Week 11 Summary — Space-Time Prediction (Bike Share Demand Forecasting)

1. The Space-Time Challenge
	•	Real-world problem: Bike rebalancing — how to get bikes where they'll be needed BEFORE demand hits.
	•	Operational question: "At 6:00 AM, which stations will run out of bikes by 8:00 AM?"
	•	Must predict demand in BOTH space AND time.

2. What Makes This Different
	•	Previous weeks (5-7): Cross-sectional prediction (predict house prices at one point in time).
	•	This week: Panel data — same stations observed over time.
	•	New features: Temporal lags (what happened last hour?), space-time interaction.

3. Panel Data Structure
	•	Definition: Data that follows the same units over multiple time periods.
	•	Cross-sectional: Each row = one observation (one snapshot in time).
	•	Panel: Each row = unit × time period (repeated observations).
	•	Example: Station × hour combinations.
	•	Key insight: Can see how demand changes WITHIN stations over time.

4. Binning Data into Time Intervals
	•	Why bin? Raw trip data has unique timestamps; need uniform intervals for aggregation.
	•	Hourly binning: All trips between 8:00-8:59 AM → "08:00" bin.
```r
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(interval60 = floor_date(ymd_hms(start_time), unit = "hour"))
```
	•	Alternative: 15-minute bins (more granular but sparser data).

5. Extracting Time Features
```r
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    week = week(interval60),            # Week of year (1-52)
    dotw = wday(interval60, label=TRUE), # Day of week (Mon, Tue, ...)
    hour = hour(interval60)             # Hour of day (0-23)
  )
```
	•	These become predictors: Rush hour indicator, weekend indicator, holiday effects.

6. Temporal Lags
	•	Core idea: Past demand predicts future demand.
	•	Spatial features (Week 6): Crimes within 500ft, distance to downtown.
	•	Temporal features (This week): Demand 1 hour ago, 2 hours ago, yesterday (24 hours ago).
	•	Intuition: If there were 15 trips at 8 AM, there will probably be ~15 trips at 9 AM.

7. Creating Lag Variables
```r
study.panel <- study.panel %>%
  arrange(from_station_id, interval60) %>%
  group_by(from_station_id) %>%
  mutate(
    lag1Hour = lag(Trip_Count, 1),    # Previous hour
    lag2Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 2),   # 2 hours ago
    lag12Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 12), # 12 hours ago
    lag1day = lag(Trip_Count, 24)     # Yesterday same time
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```
	•	Important: Lags are calculated WITHIN each station.

8. Temporal Leakage — Critical Concept
	•	Problem: Using future data to predict the past = cheating!
	•	WRONG: Train on Weeks 3-4, test on Weeks 1-2 (predicting past using future).
	•	CORRECT: Train on Weeks 1-2, test on Weeks 3-4 (predicting future using past).
	•	Real-world scenario: If it's May 15, you can only use data from May 1-14 to predict May 16+.

9. Temporal Train/Test Split
```r
# Train on early period
train <- study.panel %>%
  filter(week < 19)  # Weeks 1-2 of May

# Test on later period
test <- study.panel %>%
  filter(week >= 19) # Weeks 3-4 of May
```
	•	This mirrors operational deployment: Predict tomorrow using yesterday's patterns.

10. Comparison: Spatial CV vs Temporal Validation
	•	Week 7 (Spatial CV): Prevents spatial leakage, holds out entire neighborhoods, ensures model generalizes to new areas.
	•	This week (Temporal CV): Prevents temporal leakage, holds out future time periods, ensures model generalizes to future.
	•	Both are about out-of-sample generalization!

11. Model Progression Strategy
	•	Model 1 (Baseline): Time + Weather only (hour, day of week, temperature, precipitation).
	•	Model 2: + Temporal lags (lag1Hour, lag3Hours, lag1day).
	•	Model 3: + Spatial features (demographics, location characteristics).
	•	Model 4: + Station fixed effects (control for station-specific baselines).
	•	Model 5: + Holiday effects (Memorial Day weekend).
	•	Goal: See which features improve prediction accuracy.

12. Weather Data Integration
	•	Weather strongly affects bike share demand.
	•	Features: Temperature, precipitation, wind speed.
	•	Challenge: Match weather data to correct time intervals.

13. Evaluating Model Performance
	•	RMSE (Root Mean Square Error): Measures prediction error.
	•	MAE (Mean Absolute Error): Average absolute prediction error.
	•	Evaluate by: Station, time of day, day of week — to identify where model performs poorly.

14. Key Takeaways
	•	Panel data lets us capture both station differences AND time patterns.
	•	Temporal lags are powerful predictors (past behavior predicts future).
	•	Never use future data to predict the past — temporal validation is critical.
	•	Station fixed effects capture station-specific baseline demand.
	•	Weather and time features together explain much of demand variation.
